CAS III: Searching for Orbit Models

Value estimation on subgroup lattices — a guide to the algorithms

This page is a companion to the paper. It drops the propositions and proofs and keeps the ideas, the algorithms and the pictures: what the search is looking for, why it has to be learned, how one search step works, and how the learning loop fits together.

1 The problem

In algorithmic statistics a model for a binary string $x$ is a finite set containing it, and the best models are short to describe and fit $x$ well. CAS II reads a finite group $H$ acting on $X=\{0,1\}^n$ as such a model: the orbits of $H$ cut $X$ into cells, and the cell containing $x$ is the model it assigns. To describe $x$ with $H$ in hand, you say which cell and then where in the cell:

\[ \mathcal L_H(x)=\underbrace{\log\#\mathrm{orb}(H)}_{\text{which cell}}+\underbrace{\log|H\cdot x|}_{\text{where in the cell}} . \]

We call $\mathcal L_H(x)$ the codelength of $x$ under the coding scheme $H$. The quantity to minimise is the total two-part code: the bits needed to describe $H$ itself, written $|w|$ for a description word $w$, plus $\mathcal L_H(x)$.

Why the cost of $H$ cannot be dropped. Without it the problem collapses. Below any group $H$, the smallest codelength is reached by the stabiliser $\mathrm{Stab}_H(x)$, the group that fixes $x$. That stabiliser has $x$ as a fixed point, so it "names" $x$: it is the maximum-likelihood point mass, and the codelength is tiny only because the description of the group has absorbed the description of $x$. Charging $|w|$ makes this a bad trade, and restricting to groups of small description keeps every model found a strong one.

2 Why groups, and why learning

Groups instead of models. Searching all finite sets $A\ni x$ is hopeless and formless: there are $2^{N-1}$ of them with $N=2^n$, nothing tells a strong model from a weak one, and checking a candidate means writing down sets of up to $2^n$ points. Subgroups change three things.

  • Strong models by construction. The orbit partition of $H$ costs no more than $H$ does, so cheap groups give strong models.
  • A map. Subgroups form a lattice whose local structure is classified (O'Nan–Scott for $\mathrm{Sym}$, Aschbacher for $\mathrm{GL}$). A down move refines the partition, a sideways move relabels it, and every move has a code length.
  • Coordinates. Each group has a type and a placement, and $\mathcal L$ is read off them without touching the $2^n$ points: in $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ from double-coset tables, in $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ from ranks of matrices, since $g$ fixes the subspace $\ker(g-1)$ and Burnside's lemma gives $\#\mathrm{orb}(H)=|H|^{-1}\sum_g 2^{\dim\ker(g-1)}$.

Even the map is too big to enumerate.

ambient group$\log_2$ of the number of subgroupsmore subgroups than Go has positions ($\approx2^{566}$) for
$\mathrm{Sym}(X)$, $N=2^n$$N^2/16+O(N^{3/2})$$n\ge7$
$\mathrm{AGL}(n,2)$between those of $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ and $\mathrm{GL}(n+1,2)$$n\ge14$
$\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$between $\approx n^4/64$ and $n^4$$n\ge14$

The lattices are also wide (at least $2^N/(N+1)$ maximal subgroups below $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$) and deep. So the answer is the one of AlphaGo and AlphaZero: a learned value function judges positions that cannot be searched to the end, and a tree search spends computation where that judgement is uncertain. Three things differ from Go: the game has one player and dense rewards; branching is tamed only because moves cost bits (a budget of $\varepsilon$ bits leaves at most $(\varepsilon+1)2^\varepsilon$ reachable groups); and a Go engine knows when it has won, while a model searcher never knows how close it is — the target, the sufficiency line $\alpha+\beta=C(x)$, is uncomputable.

3 Staying with strong models

Restricting to cheap hypotheses is the point of the cost, but "cheap" has no clean description in lattice terms. The cheap subgroups $L_\varepsilon=\{H: C(H)\le\varepsilon\}$ are few, scattered at every height, closed neither upward nor downward, and membership cannot even be decided. What can be decided is a sound inner version: start from a few structured seeds with short codes, give every move a code length, and keep the groups reachable within the budget. This is the strong sublattice $B_\varepsilon$.

4 The search as a decision process

A state is a description word $w$ (with its group $H_w$), the string $x$, the cost weight $\lambda$ and the remaining budget $b$. The actions are

  • Down$(M)$: move to a maximal subgroup $M$ of $H$;
  • Side$(\gamma)$: conjugate by a cheap letter $\gamma$ (a bit flip, a coordinate swap, a transvection), giving an isomorphic group in a new position;
  • Stop.

Each move has a code length $|\Delta w|$ and is allowed only if it fits the budget. The potential of a state is

\[ \Phi_\lambda(w,x)=\lambda|w|+\mathcal L_{H_w}(x), \]

and the reward of a move is the decrease of the potential: positive when the move shortens the weighted description of $x$ by more than it costs to describe the move. Stop earns nothing and there is no discounting, so the return from a state is simply the number of weighted bits removed between it and the stopping point.

5 What the value function measures

With these rewards the optimal value of a state has a plain meaning:

\[ V^*(s)=\Phi(s)-\min_{s'\text{ reachable from }s}\Phi(s'), \]

the gap between the model you have and the best model you could still reach. At the root, the best model of $x$ in the whole hypothesis class is read off the value. Model search is value estimation.

The value can never be computed exactly at interesting sizes, but it can be bracketed. From above it is bounded by a closed-form quantity $\overline V=\delta_H-\delta_{\mathrm{Stab}_H(x)}$, computed from the group alone (here $\delta_H$ measures how far $H$ is from acting freely). From below, every path actually explored gives a certified improvement. The learned network is squeezed in between.

Three levels of knowing. The distance to the sufficiency line is uncomputable (it needs $C(x)$). The optimal value $V^*$ is computable but intractable (a minimum over a finite but astronomical set). The learned value $\widehat V_\theta$ is cheap, trained on certified lower bounds and capped by the closed-form ceiling. The value function estimates the distance to sufficiency in the only sense available: as the distance that can actually be travelled.

6 The pipeline

7 Evaluating and proposing

Every algorithm below calls the same two subroutines: one scores a state, the other suggests where to go next.

Algorithm 1 Evaluate$(w,x,\lambda)$
  1. Get $H=H_w$ and its order. Compute $\#\mathrm{orb}(H)$ by Burnside's lemma over conjugacy classes — never by listing orbits.
  2. Compute the stabiliser $S=\mathrm{Stab}_H(x)$; then $|H\cdot x|=|H|/|S|$.
  3. Return the codelength $\mathcal L$, the potential $\Phi=\lambda|w|+\mathcal L$, the ceiling $\overline V$, the floor $\Phi_{\rm low}=\lambda|w|+\log\#\mathrm{orb}(S)$ used for pruning, and the invariant features of $(H,x)$ for the network.

A large group has astronomically many maximal subgroups, and random ones almost never relate to $x$. Candidates are therefore generated from $x$, but each is charged its code length, which does not depend on $x$.

Algorithm 1b Propose$(s,k)$
  1. Interval moves: for blocks of $H$ on the orbit of $x$ that contain $x$, the block stabiliser — these never increase $\mathcal L$.
  2. Stabiliser-preserving moves: conjugates of maximal subgroups that keep as much of $\mathrm{Stab}_H(x)$ as possible.
  3. Structural moves specific to the ambient group (subspaces built from $x$, summands that contain $x$, …).
  4. Sideways moves by the cheap letters, and a few random moves for exploration.
  5. Drop moves over budget; rank by the policy $\pi_\theta$ (once it exists) and keep the best $k$.

8 Monte Carlo with exploring starts

The first phase needs no planner: run episodes, record the potential at every visited state, and regress a value network on what the episodes found.

Algorithm 2 Episode$(\widehat V_\theta,\eta)$
  1. Draw a training string $x$: either a planted string (a fixed point of a randomly reached cheap group, so a good model is known to exist) or a uniform control string.
  2. Start at the root or at a random admissible word (charged) — the exploring start.
  3. Repeat: evaluate the state; collect candidates plus Stop; take a random action first and with probability $\eta$, otherwise the greedy one, maximising reward $+\ \widehat V_\theta(\text{next})$; record $\Phi_t$.
  4. Stop on Stop and return the recorded trajectory.

From a trajectory $s_0,\dots,s_T$ two targets can be read:

\[ G_t=\Phi_t-\Phi_T\quad\text{(where this episode stopped)},\qquad L_t=\Phi_t-\min_{t'\ge t}\Phi_{t'}\quad\text{(the best stopping point on the path)}. \]

$L_t$ is the one to train on. It is a certified lower bound on $V^*$ for data from any policy, including a random one, so even the first random episodes give valid targets. $G_t$ is not: with a random policy that never stops, every chain runs to the trivial group and $G_t$ says nothing about what lies below the state.

9 Monte Carlo lattice search (MCLS)

MCLS is Monte Carlo tree search adapted to the subgroup lattice. It spends a fixed amount of computation on one string, growing a small part of the lattice in memory and repeatedly deciding which part to grow next. Four things distinguish it from game-playing MCTS:

  • a graph, not a tree: one node per subgroup, shared by every path that reaches it (transpositions);
  • max-backups: a node's worth is the best model below it, not the average — there is no opponent and no chance;
  • progressive widening from $x$-guided proposals, because the branching is enormous;
  • pruning by a provable lattice bound.

Each node $v$ stores its codelength $\mathcal L_v$, a visit count, and two numbers:

  • $\mu_v$, the best potential actually found below $v$ (path-independent: cost from $v$ plus codelength), so $\mathcal L_v-\mu_v$ is a certified lower bound on $V^*(v)$;
  • $\tilde\mu_v$, the same with unexplored leaves filled in by the network's guess — this one steers the search.
Algorithm 3 MCLS$(x,\lambda,\varepsilon,K)$
Repeat $K$ simulations from the root:
  1. Select. From the root, move to the child maximising \[\frac{\mathcal L_v-\lambda e_{vc}-\tilde\mu_c}{\max(\overline V_v,1)}+c_{\rm puct}\,\pi_\theta(c\mid v)\frac{\sqrt{N_v}}{1+N_c},\] until a node has fewer than $\lceil c_wN_v^{\alpha}\rceil$ children (progressive widening).
  2. Expand. Add the next proposed child; if it is already in the table (reached by another path), link to it.
  3. Prune. If cost so far $+$ edge cost $+\log\#\mathrm{orb}(\mathrm{Stab}(x))$ below the child is no better than the best found, $\mu_\rho$, mark the edge pruned.
  4. Evaluate. New node: $\mu\leftarrow\mathcal L$, $\tilde\mu\leftarrow\mathcal L-\widehat V_\theta$; optionally run a quick random descent.
  5. Back up. Up the path, $\mu_u\leftarrow\min(\mu_u,\ \lambda e_{uc}+\mu_c)$ and likewise for $\tilde\mu$; increment visit counts.
Return the best model ($\mu$ at the root), the archive of all nodes with their profile points, and training targets: $\mathcal L_v-\mu_v$ for the value, child visit counts for the policy.
MCLS versus following the network greedily. Greedy descent (pick the move with the best reward $+\widehat V$) is optimal if the network is perfect, but its commitments are irreversible and its errors compound. MCLS uses the same network to decide where to look, then checks: it backtracks, corrects early misjudgements with what it finds, and reports only results backed by real groups. In the training loop MCLS improves on the network, and the network is trained on what MCLS finds — the AlphaZero pattern.

10 The value and policy networks

  • Inputs. The group as a padded, masked generating set (in $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$, $n\times n$ binary matrices; in Burnside coordinates, the type and placement); the string $x$ as a raw binary vector; optionally the invariant features of $(H,x)$, and $\lambda$, $b$.
  • Encoders. A small CNN per generator, a Set Transformer with induced set attention, masked mean pooling; an MLP for $x$; a fusion MLP to a trunk vector.
  • Heads. Value: $\widehat V_\theta=\sigma(\cdot)\cdot\overline V$, which respects the ceiling by construction. Policy: an MLP scoring $[\,z,e_{H_c}\,]$ for each candidate child, softmax over candidates.
  • What must be learned. Two generating sets of the same group look different, so training is augmented with Nielsen moves and redundant generators; conjugation symmetry is taught by augmenting with random relabellings of the generators and $x$ together.
  • Losses. Huber loss on certified targets ($L_t$, MCLS values, relabelled targets), regressed as a fraction of $\overline V$; cross-entropy of the policy against MCLS visit counts.

An implementation for $\mathrm{GL}(40,2)$ takes up to 15 generators, a three-stage CNN per matrix to 256 dimensions, four Set Transformer layers (8 heads, 32 inducing points), and fusion widths 512/256/128. A larger variant reads the generators and the string as token streams with two Transformers of width 768 and about $10^8$ parameters.

11 Sharing exploration across strings

A hypothesis is a coding scheme for every string at once. Split the potential as

\[ \Phi_\lambda(w,x)=\underbrace{\lambda|w|+\log\#\mathrm{orb}(H_w)}_{\text{same for every }x}+\underbrace{\log|H_w\cdot x|}_{\text{depends on }x}. \]

The expensive work — computing maximal subgroups, codes and orbit counts — does not depend on the string. So a graph explored while searching for one string gives valid training targets for every string: for each $x$, one backward pass over the explored graph gives

\[ V_D(w,x)=\Phi(w,x)-\min_{u\text{ explored below }w}\Phi(u,x)\ \le\ V^*(w,x), \]

a certified lower bound. This is hindsight relabelling with the string as the goal.

Algorithm 4 SharedTrain$(\{x_1,\dots,x_B\},\Lambda)$
  1. Actors (string-independent): expand the lattice, guided by some string or a batch criterion; store each node's code length and orbit count once.
  2. Scorers (embarrassingly parallel): for each new node and each string, compute the height $\log|H\cdot x|$ and the ceiling $\overline V$.
  3. DP: one bottom-up pass per string and weight gives $V_D$ for every node.
  4. Learner: regress on $V_D$ for the strings that guided exploration; for the others only penalise predictions outside $[V_D,\overline V]$ (their bound may be loose).

Sharing helps most near the top of the lattice, where coarse groups are useful for many strings; deep nodes become specific to one string. The shared graph acts like an opening book; the end of each search is still a per-string MCLS.

12 The training loop

Algorithm 5 Train
  1. Phase A — bootstrap. Random-policy episodes first; record $\Phi_t$ at every state. Then repeat: regress $\widehat V_\theta$ on $L_t$; run episodes with the new network on planted and control strings.
  2. Phase B — search and distil. Repeat: run MCLS on a batch of strings with the current networks; add value targets $\mathcal L_v-\mu_v$ and policy targets from visit counts; insert the searched nodes into the shared graph and add relabelled targets for the whole batch; update on a replay buffer. Stop when validation regret stops improving.
  3. Phase C — optional, amortised MDL. Fit an $x$-blind prior $q$ to the move sequences of the best descriptions found, freeze it, use $-\log q$ as the code, and repeat Phase B. Hypotheses that were useful across many strings become cheaper to describe.

Ground truth on small lattices. When the whole lattice below a root fits in memory, optimal values are computed exactly by dynamic programming from the bottom up. This validates learned values and searches on $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb F_2^2)=S_4$ (30 subgroups), on any Burnside hypothesis with a small abstract group, and on $\mathrm{GL}(3,2)$ (179 subgroups) and $\mathrm{GL}(4,2)\cong A_8$.

Two ambient groups

13 All permutations: Burnside coordinates

With $\mathrm{Sym}(X)$ every partition is symmetric, so the search can in principle express every model (any set $B\ni x$ is a cell of $\mathrm{Sym}(B)\times\mathrm{Sym}(X\setminus B)$). Two caveats: reaching a set requires describing it cheaply, and in $\mathrm{Sym}$ the information of a model tends to sit in its placement, not in its symmetry. The search therefore works with descriptions of groups in coordinates.

Coordinates. A hypothesis is an abstract group $H$ from a library, a type $b=\sum_j a_j[H/K_j]$ (how many copies of each transitive $H$-set are laid out on $X$), a current subgroup $L\le H$, and a placement word $\sigma$. Then everything is a table lookup:

\[ \mathcal L=\log\sum_j a_j\,|L\backslash H/K_j|+\log|L:L\cap K_x|, \]

a count of double cosets plus an index. The lattice below a hypothesis is just $\mathrm{Sub}(H)$ — small, fully tabulated, and independent of $n$.

Algorithm 6 EvaluateBurnside
  1. Apply the placement letters in reverse to one point: $y=\sigma^{-1}x$. (Never build a permutation of $2^n$ points.)
  2. Locate the summand and coset of $y$ in the layout; this gives the stabiliser $K_x$ and $S=L\cap K_x$.
  3. Read the double-coset counts for $L$ and $S$ from tables; return $\mathcal L$, $\overline V$, $\Phi$, $\Phi_{\rm low}$ and features.

Seeds are the natural actions on the cube, each described in $O(\log n)$ bits: coordinate permutations $S_n$ (orbits = weight classes, giving the familiar code by Hamming weight), block products $S_k\times S_{n-k}$, translation subgroups (subcubes), $\mathrm{AGL}(n,2)$ and $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$. MCLS keys nodes by $(H,[b],L,j,\text{double coset of }x)$, so positions of $x$ in the same double coset share a node.

14 Linear symmetry: GL(n,2)

Here the cells are $\{0\}$ and the linearly homogeneous sets; affine subspaces are cells of cheap hypotheses. A placement costs at most $n^2$ bits, so the space is small enough to search — and, by the same token, provably blind to some simple structure.

Evaluation is linear algebra. An element $u$ fixes $\ker(u-I)$, of size $2^{n-\mathrm{rank}(u-I)}$, so

\[ \#\mathrm{orb}(H)=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{\text{classes }C}|C|\,2^{\,n-\mathrm{rank}(c_C-I)}, \]

point stabilisers come from Schreier–Sims, and $\mathrm{Fix}(H)$ is a null space. Orbits on $\mathbb F_2^n$ are never listed.

Seeds: block-diagonal groups on coordinate intervals, pointwise stabilisers of coordinate subspaces, permutation matrices, the unitriangular group, Singer cycles, symplectic groups. Moves: restriction to maximal subgroups, and relabelling by transvections and coordinate swaps. Proposals are built from $x$: stabilisers of $\langle x\rangle$, of coordinate subspaces containing $x$, of $\mathrm{Fix}(\mathrm{Stab}_H(x))$, and transvections that move $x$ into larger fixed spaces.

What to expect. There are strings whose best models are affine, and planted strings have near-sufficient reachable models, so the search has targets. But any polynomial budget gives a class that is blind to some random-looking yet simple strings: a small root value means "no linear structure found", not "$x$ is random". And a search that stalls inside an interval with no cheap halving block may have found a real plateau of the profile.

15 The two searches together

$\mathrm{GL}(n,2)\le\mathrm{AGL}(n,2)\le\mathrm{Sym}(X)$, and a linear group has the same orbits and the same $\mathcal L$ viewed as a permutation group. The linear search is the down-set of one seed of the permutation search, so the interesting quantity is the difference. If both find a near-sufficient cheap model, $x$ has linear-symmetric structure; if only the permutation search does, its structure is simple but not linear-symmetric, and the cost split of the permutation model says whether it is a genuine symmetry or a named set.

Outlook. The paper gives the theory and the algorithms and reports no experiments. The next step is to implement MCLS with the networks above for both ambient groups, validate against exact values on small lattices and on planted strings, and then run at sizes where the lattice can no longer be enumerated.
